facts.statement: Asteracanthus was one of the largest known hybodonts, growing up to 2 to 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Asteracanthus was among the largest known hybodontiforms, reaching a length of 2 - 3 m.

facts.statement: The teeth of Asteracanthus were high-crowned and multi-cusped.
facts.quote: The dentition of Astercanthus is high crowned and multicusped.

facts.statement: The fin spines of Asteracanthus were covered in tubercles instead of the ribbing found in other hybodonts.
facts.quote: Like Strophodus, the fin spines are covered in tubercles, rather than the ribbing typical of other hybodont fin spines.

facts.statement: Fossils of Asteracanthus have been found in Europe, including Germany, Switzerland, England, and France.
facts.quote: The genus as currently circumscribed dates from the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) to Early Cretaceous (Valanginian) of Europe, including Germany, Switzerland, England and France.

facts.statement: Asteracanthus was adapted for open marine environments and likely swam just above the seafloor.
facts.quote: The genus seems to have been adapted for open marine conditions and likely had an epibenthic habit (swimming just above the seafloor).

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Asteracanthus used its teeth for grasping prey, with side teeth adapted for crushing.
facts.quote: The teeth are suggested to have been adapted for grasping, with the teeth at the sides of the mouth serving a crushing function.

facts.statement: Asteracanthus likely fed on a diverse diet including fish, crustaceans, echinoderms, molluscs, and cephalopods like belemnites.
facts.quote: Asteracanthus was probably adapted for feeding on a wide range of prey, ranging from moderately hard shelled to soft-bodied, likely including fish, crustaceans, echinoderms, hard shelled molluscs and cephalopods like belemnites.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Asteracanthus may have scavenged on marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Teeth of Asteracanthus found with the remains of marine reptiles suggest that it may have also engaged in scavenging.

facts.statement: A complete skeleton of Asteracanthus was described in 2021 from Late Jurassic Solnhofen Limestone.
facts.quote: A complete skeleton was described in 2021 from the Late Jurassic (Tithonian) aged Solnhofen Limestone.

facts.statement: Asteracanthus is classified as a member of the class Chondrichthyes, order Hybodontiformes, and family Hybodontidae.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Chondrichthyes ordo: Hybodontiformes familia: Hybodontidae genus: Asteracanthus

facts.statement: The genus Asteracanthus is now considered distinct from Strophodus, with its teeth being more similar to those of Hybodus and Egertonodus.
facts.quote: Previously considered synonymous, the genus Strophodus (Middle Triassic-Late Cretaceous) is now considered distinct, with the teeth of Asteracanthus having more in common with Hybodus and Egertonodus.

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Asteracanthus as Acrodontinae and the family as Acrodontidae.
